text: Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their array.

versions.text: So the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their array.
versions.explanation: The rendering is accurate; "Thus" gives a slightly more resonant cadence for oral reading at this summarizing sentence than the lighter "So," which is better reserved for narrative sequence. "All their array" is retained as a faithful rendering of the Hebrew term for host/array, and the closing phrase keeps the natural falling rhythm of the Hebrew line.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a passive verb form (pual) of the root meaning "to complete, bring to an end": literally "and the heavens and the earth were completed." "Thus" renders the connecting waw, which here draws a conclusion rather than adding a new event — the sentence rounds off the six days of chapter 1. The agent is left unnamed, though it is obviously God; some renderings supply "God had finished the heavens and the earth," but the passive keeps the Hebrew's quiet, summarizing tone. The final phrase, literally "and all their host," is rendered "all their array": "host" in older English usage means an army or a vast multitude, while "array" preserves both the military overtone and the sense of ordered ranks, and it falls more naturally on the ear when read aloud. Placing it after a comma at the end lets the sentence close with a cadence, mirroring the way the Hebrew adds the phrase as a final flourish.

The verb here (root k-l-h) is the same root used in the next verse of God "finishing" his work; the passive in v. 1 and the active in v. 2 form a deliberate pair. The noun tsava' ("host, army, service") is a military word, used elsewhere of Israel's fighting units and of the stars as ranked troops of heaven. The suffix is plural — "their host" — covering both heaven and earth, so the phrase sweeps up everything that fills them, not only the stars. "The heavens and the earth" is a merism, a pairing of opposites that means "everything," and its repetition here echoes the opening words of chapter 1, framing the creation account.

The verse insists that creation is complete: nothing is lacking, nothing left over. This completeness is the ground for the rest that follows. That the sun, moon, and stars belong to God's "host" is theologically pointed — the heavenly bodies and any heavenly beings are creatures under command, not rival powers. Later Scripture speaks of "the LORD of hosts," and of God calling out the starry host by name; readers in both Jewish and Christian tradition have heard in "all their array" an inclusion of the angelic ranks as well as the visible sky.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, sun, moon, and stars were widely worshipped as deities, and their movements were read for omens. To list them simply as part of the "array" that God completed is a striking demotion: they are staff, not gods. The military image of a heavenly army would also have been familiar from royal and imperial imagery, where a great king was pictured surrounded by ordered ranks of servants.

The early Greek translation renders the final phrase with a word meaning "ordered arrangement, adornment" (kosmos), interpreting the "host" as the ordered beauty of the universe rather than as an army; this reading stands behind the later use of "the cosmos" for the created world. Some ancient witnesses read "the heaven" as a singular and one traditional Aramaic rendering paraphrases "all their hosts" as "all their multitudes." These are interpretive differences; the consonantal Hebrew text is stable.

In Jewish practice this verse begins the passage (Gen 2:1–3) recited or sung at the start of the Sabbath — over the cup at the Friday evening blessing and in the synagogue service. Because of this, the verse is among the most frequently spoken lines of the Torah in the home, and translations meant for reading aloud are often shaped with that use in mind.

text: By the seventh day God had finished the work he had done, and on the seventh day he rested from all the work he had done.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb form (a simple past, "and God finished") literally says that God finished his work "on the seventh day," which seems to place activity on the very day of rest. Hebrew narrative past tenses can carry the force of an English pluperfect, so the rendering "By the seventh day God had finished" states that the work was already complete when the seventh day arrived. Other defensible renderings are "On the seventh day God finished the work he had done" (understanding the act of ceasing itself as the completion) or "God had completed, on the seventh day, the work he had done." The repeated phrase "the work he had done" is kept identical in both halves of the verse, since the Hebrew deliberately repeats it word for word, and the two occurrences of "the seventh day" are likewise preserved rather than smoothed away, because the repetition gives the sentence its balanced, chant-like rhythm.

The verb translated "rested" is shavat, whose basic sense is "cease, stop, desist" rather than "take a nap" or "recover strength." It is the root behind the noun shabbat, so the verse plants a play on words that the seventh-day theme will harvest: God "shabbat-ed" on the seventh day. A different Hebrew verb (nuach) means rest in the sense of settling down or being refreshed, and it is not the one used here. The noun melakhah, "work," denotes assigned task, craft, or occupation — it is the ordinary word for a person's business or handiwork, not the word for toil or drudgery.

God's ceasing is not recovery from exhaustion; the text says nothing about fatigue, only about completion. The seventh day is thus not a gap in God's activity but the crown of the creation account: the goal toward which the six days move. Interpreters have drawn different conclusions from this. Some see here the founding of the Sabbath as a creation ordinance built into the fabric of the world for all humanity; others read it as a pattern later given legal form for Israel alone. Christian writers have also read God's rest as an unfinished invitation, a rest that God's people are still called to enter.

Several ancient witnesses — including the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Greek tradition, and the Syriac — read "on the sixth day God finished the work," evidently to remove the appearance that God worked on the seventh. The Hebrew manuscript tradition uniformly reads "seventh," and the harder reading is almost certainly the original, with "sixth" arising as a smoothing correction. The translation follows the Hebrew and resolves the difficulty through the tense of the verb instead.

No other ancient Near Eastern creation account culminates in a day of ceasing tied to a recurring seven-day rhythm. In neighbouring literature the gods rest after establishing a temple or after humans are made to bear their labour; here the rest belongs to a calendar that ordinary people will keep. The word melakhah later became the technical rabbinic term for the categories of activity forbidden on the Sabbath, precisely because of its use in this verse.

This verse, together with the surrounding verses of the passage, forms the opening of the Sabbath blessing over wine sung in Jewish homes on Friday evening, and it is also woven into synagogue prayers for the Sabbath. Its measured repetitions make it well suited to being chanted aloud.

text: Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creation he had done.

footnotes.text: The final clause reads literally "which God created to do/make" (asher bara elohim la'asot) — a compact Hebrew construction in which the infinitive la'asot follows the verb "created" without an obvious object. Rendering it word for word ("which God created to make") is opaque in English, so the phrase is treated as a single idea and given as "the work of creation he had done," letting the two verbs stand together as one comprehensive expression for God's creative activity. Other defensible readings take the infinitive as purposive ("which God created so that it might be made," i.e. creation set going to continue producing) or as a hendiadys ("which God had created and made"). "Made it holy" is preferred over "sanctified" or "hallowed" because it keeps the plain, sayable rhythm of the line for reading aloud, while carrying the same sense of setting apart. "Then" opens the verse to mark the sequence after the resting of verse 2, matching the Hebrew narrative verb chain.

The verb shavat means to cease, stop, desist — not to recover from fatigue; it is the root behind the noun shabbat, so the seventh day is named by what happens on it before the word "Sabbath" is ever used. Va-yeqaddesh is the causative-declarative (piel) form of the root q-d-sh, "to be set apart"; this is the first occurrence of holiness language in the Bible, and strikingly it is applied to a stretch of time rather than to a place, an object, or a person. Note also that this is the third blessing in the chapter's opening story (after the sea creatures and humanity), and the only one pronounced over a day.

The Sabbath is here grounded not in law but in creation itself: the day is blessed and set apart before any commandment is given and before any covenant people exists, a point later taken up when the Sabbath command is anchored in these six days and the seventh. Interpreters have long noticed that the seventh day alone lacks the closing formula "and there was evening and there was morning," and have read this as a hint that God's rest is not shut off at sundown but remains open — a reading developed both in rabbinic tradition and in the New Testament idea of a rest that still stands open for God's people. The verse also makes holiness a matter of time rather than territory, so that the sanctity of the day is available to anyone, anywhere.

In the wider ancient Near Eastern world, stories of creation often end with the deity coming to rest — typically in a newly built temple, where the god's rest signifies settled, secure rule over the ordered world. Genesis shares that shape while pointedly leaving out the temple, the cult image, and the servile labor of humanity: the cosmos itself is the space in which God takes up rest. A recurring seventh-day observance for the whole population, including slaves and resident foreigners, has no clear parallel in the surrounding cultures and became one of the most visible marks of Israelite and later Jewish life.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable across the manuscript tradition; it closes with a paragraph marker (petuchah) in the traditional scribal layout, dividing the creation account from what follows. The ancient Greek tradition renders the last clause with "which God began to do/make," apparently reading the infinitive as inceptive. In verse 2 several ancient witnesses read "sixth day" where the Hebrew has "seventh," evidently to avoid the impression that God finished work on the day of rest; that variant does not affect the present verse.

Verses 1–3 are recited over the cup at the Friday evening Kiddush that opens the Sabbath in Jewish homes, so this line has been spoken weekly for millennia as a household blessing. In Christian usage the passage is a standard reading at vigils and at services marking creation and rest, and it stands behind the shaping of a weekly day set apart for worship.

text: This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, on the day the LORD God made the earth and the heavens.

versions.text: This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day the LORD God made earth and heaven.
versions.explanation: "In the day" is an archaic Hebraism that reads awkwardly aloud; "on the day" is idiomatic English and preserves the temporal sense of בְּיוֹם. Adding the articles to "the earth and the heavens" smooths the closing cadence while keeping the deliberate reversal of the word order from the first half of the verse.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word *toledot* literally means "begettings" or "generations," the offspring or outcome of something. Since heavens and earth do not literally beget children, "account" is used here to convey what the term signals: the story of what came forth from something. Alternatives include "generations," "origins," "history," or "these are the descendants of." The phrase *be-hibbare'am* ("when they were created") is a passive infinitive that echoes the verb *bara* used in 1:1, and the rendering "on the day" preserves the Hebrew idiom *be-yom*, which in ordinary usage functions simply as "when" rather than marking a strict twenty-four-hour period; some render it "at the time when." The word order "the earth and the heavens" in the second half deliberately reverses "the heavens and the earth" in the first half, and the translation keeps that reversal rather than smoothing it out.

*Elleh toledot* ("these are the generations of") is a structural formula that recurs some eleven times through Genesis, marking the seams between major sections. It normally introduces what follows rather than summarizing what precedes, which is why most readers take this line as the heading of the garden narrative that begins here. The mirrored word order — heavens/earth, then earth/heavens — forms a chiasm that closes the first creation account and pivots the focus downward to the ground, where the next verses begin. In the Masoretic manuscript tradition the letter *he* in *be-hibbare'am* is written small, a scribal peculiarity noted by copyists for centuries; ancient interpreters played on it, reading the consonants as "with *he* he created them" or rearranging them to spell *be-Avraham*, "for Abraham's sake."

This is the first place in Scripture where the personal covenant name of God, rendered here as LORD in capital letters, appears joined to the general word for God (*Elohim*). The compound title binds the transcendent Creator of chapter 1 to the intimate, garden-walking God of chapter 2 — they are one and the same. Critical scholarship has long read the shift in divine names as evidence of distinct literary sources woven together; the received text, however, presents the two accounts as complementary panels, the first cosmic in scope, the second focused on humanity and the ground. The idiomatic "on the day" here, covering the whole span of creative work, has often been cited in discussions of how the six days of chapter 1 are to be understood.

Genealogical and origin formulas of this kind were a standard way of organizing narrative in the ancient Near East, where family lines carried legal weight and a people's identity was told through who came from whom. Applying such a formula to heaven and earth is striking: the cosmos itself is given a lineage, and the whole story of the world is told in the shape of a family record. Mesopotamian creation traditions likewise open by naming the time "when" things were not yet made, a rhetorical pattern the following verses also follow.

The Greek tradition renders the opening as "This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth," adding the word "book," a phrasing later echoed in New Testament genealogical language. Some Greek and other ancient witnesses read simply "God" rather than the compound divine title throughout this section, apparently harmonizing with chapter 1. The Hebrew consonantal text is otherwise stable here; the small *he* is a graphic scribal feature rather than a variant reading.

text: No shrub of the field had yet appeared on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to work the ground.

footnotes.text: In Hebrew verses 4b–7 form one long, winding sentence: a series of 'not yet' clauses leading up to the main statement in verse 7. For oral reading this has been broken into shorter, self-standing sentences, so this verse stands alone as a description of the world before rain and before human labour. Some renderings keep the suspended construction ('When no shrub of the field was yet on the earth... then the LORD God formed the man'); the sense is the same, but the shorter units read more naturally aloud. 'Had yet appeared' translates a verb that literally means 'was' or 'existed'; 'appeared' is used because English needs a verb of emerging with 'shrub'. 'Field' renders a word that can also mean open country; 'the earth' and 'the ground' render two different Hebrew words, kept distinct here because the second one (adamah) is the word from which the man is formed in verse 7. 'Sent rain' renders a single causative verb, 'to make it rain', whose subject is God himself.

The word rendered 'shrub' (siach) is rare, occurring only a handful of times in the Hebrew Bible, always of wild desert scrub that offers scant shelter or food. 'Plant' (esev) is the ordinary word for green herbage, and elsewhere for grain and cultivated greens. The adverb terem, 'not yet', is regularly followed by a verb in the imperfect even when the reference is to past time, which is why English must supply 'had yet'. The closing clause turns on a deliberate sound-play: adam ('man') has no work to do on the adamah ('ground') — a pairing that runs through the whole chapter and returns in 3:19, 'until you return to the ground, for from it you were taken.' The blunt Hebrew phrase is literally 'and man — none', using the particle of non-existence.

The verse names two lacks — no rain from above, no worker from below — and thus frames humanity's role from the outset as partnership in the flourishing of the land rather than mere consumption of it. Readers have long noted that the order of events here differs in emphasis from chapter 1, where vegetation precedes humanity; many understand this passage as describing not all plant life but specifically the growth that depends on rainfall and cultivation, that is, the world of agriculture that begins with the man in the garden. Others read the two accounts as complementary perspectives rather than a single chronological sequence. The mention of the ground needing to be worked also quietly anticipates chapter 3, where that same labour becomes toil among thorns and thistles.

In the land of the Bible, agriculture depended on seasonal rain rather than on the great river systems of Egypt and Mesopotamia, where irrigation canals carried water to the fields. The pairing of divine rain with human labour therefore reflects lived experience: a farmer could plough, sow and weed, but the harvest hung on rains that only God could give. The distinction between wild scrub of the open country and the cultivated green plants of the field would have been immediately intelligible to an agrarian audience.

Ancient versions show minor variation here. Some Greek witnesses read 'all the green of the field' and 'all the grass of the field', smoothing the two rare Hebrew terms into a more familiar pair, and some manuscripts and versions vary in whether the divine name appears as 'the LORD God' or simply 'God' throughout this section. None of these differences affects the sense of the verse, and the traditional Hebrew text is followed here.

text: But a mist would rise from the earth and water the whole surface of the ground.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a simple conjunction ("and"), but the clause functions as a contrast to the previous verse's statement that no rain had fallen; "But" makes that contrast audible for a listener. The verb form is imperfect, which here describes repeated or customary action in past time, hence "would rise" rather than a single event ("a mist rose") or a future ("a mist will rise"). The rare noun rendered "mist" has also been translated "stream," "spring," "flow," or "flood" (see the linguistic and text-critical notes); "mist" is chosen because it fits the immediate context of moisture reaching "the whole surface" of the soil and keeps the gentle, reading-friendly cadence of the line. The second verb is causative, literally "caused to drink," i.e. gave water to; "water" preserves this in ordinary English.

The noun 'ed occurs only twice in the Hebrew Bible: here and in Job 36:27, where it stands in a description of rain and clouds. Its rarity is why translators differ so widely. Some connect it to a root meaning "to rise, go up" and understand vapor or mist; others link it to Akkadian edû, a term for subterranean or seasonal flood-water, and so read "stream" or "underground flow." Note also the sustained wordplay of the chapter between 'adam ("man") and 'adamah ("ground"), the word used here for the soil that is watered; the same pairing drives verse 7. The verb hishqah is the causative (Hifil) of the root "to drink" and is regularly used of watering flocks, gardens, and fields.

The Greek and Latin traditions read a "spring" or "fountain" rising from the earth rather than a mist, and some later interpreters followed them; the Hebrew manuscript tradition is uniform in the consonants, so the variation reflects different understandings of a rare word rather than a different text.

The verse quietly answers the problem posed in verse 5: rain had not yet come and no one worked the soil, yet the ground was not left dry. Water arrives from below rather than from above, wholly as God's provision and without human labor or cultivation. Readers have drawn different lessons: some see a picture of an initial, pre-rain order of creation; others read it as the setting of the stage for the garden of verses 8-14, where God plants and irrigates before entrusting the ground to the man.

In the ancient Near East, agriculture depended either on seasonal rainfall, as in the hill country of Canaan, or on river flooding and irrigation channels, as in Mesopotamia and Egypt. A picture of water welling up from the earth to soak the whole surface of the soil would have evoked the second, irrigated kind of land — fertile ground made productive by water rising and spreading rather than falling from the sky.

text: Then the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb here (wayyîṣer) is the word used for a potter shaping clay, so "formed" is preferred over the more general "made" or "created." The noun hā'ādām carries the definite article and is rendered "the man" rather than the proper name "Adam"; the name proper does not clearly emerge until later in the narrative. Some render it "the human" or "humankind" to keep the generic sense. "Dust of the ground" smooths a compact Hebrew phrase that literally reads "dust from the ground"; "soil" or "earth" are equally possible for 'ădāmāh. The closing phrase nephesh ḥayyāh has traditionally been rendered "a living soul," but since the same expression describes animals earlier in the creation account, "a living being" better conveys the sense of an animated, breathing creature. For oral reading the verse is carried by three linked beats — formed, breathed, became — with light punctuation so the sentence can be spoken in one breath-arc.

The verse turns on a sound-play impossible to reproduce in English: 'ādām ("man") is drawn from 'ădāmāh ("ground"), rather as if one said "the human from the humus" or "the earthling from the earth." Note also the shift in vocabulary for breath: nĕshāmāh ("breath") here, alongside the more common rûaḥ elsewhere; the related verb wayyippaḥ suggests a forceful, intimate blowing, as into embers or a flute. The spelling of the opening verb with a doubled yod is unusual and was much discussed by early Jewish commentators, who read it as a hint of a twofold forming or of two inclinations within the human heart. "Nostrils" translates a dual noun ("his two nostrils"), the same word that elsewhere means "face" or "anger."

This verse holds together two truths that later theology often separated: humanity is wholly of the earth, and humanity is wholly dependent on God's breath. The human is not described as receiving a soul as a separable part, but as becoming a living being through the divine breathing; body and life are one gift. Because the phrase "living being" is used of animals too, what distinguishes humanity here is not a different substance but the direct, personal act of God bending near to breathe. Later reflection contrasts this first man, drawn from dust and given life, with a second and final Adam who gives life. The dust also anticipates mortality: the one formed from dust will be told he returns to it.

Divine craftsmanship in clay was a familiar image across the ancient Near East: Egyptian texts picture a creator god shaping human beings on a potter's wheel, and Mesopotamian accounts describe humanity fashioned from clay, sometimes mixed with the blood or spittle of the gods. Against that background this account is notable for what it omits — no divine substance is kneaded into the mixture, and no human being is made to relieve the gods of labor. The potter's craft itself would have been everyday knowledge to the first hearers, who watched wet clay pressed and turned into vessels that could just as easily be shattered.

The Greek tradition renders the final phrase with words later quoted in the New Testament discussion of the first and last Adam, and some early witnesses expand the verse slightly with connective particles. Such variants affect style rather than substance; the consonantal Hebrew text is stable here, apart from the well-known unusual spelling of the first verb, which the manuscript tradition preserves consistently.

The verse has long shaped prayers at the beginning and the end of life: morning prayers in the Jewish tradition bless God for the breath placed within, and funeral rites in many Christian traditions echo the dust of this verse in committing the body to the ground while entrusting the breath to God. It is also a common reading at services concerning creation, human dignity, and the beginning of Lent.

text: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and there he placed the man he had formed.

versions.text: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he placed the man he had formed.
versions.explanation: The back-to-back prepositional phrases "in Eden, in the east" create a slight stumble when read aloud. "toward the east" renders מִקֶּדֶם just as accurately (directional/locational sense) while smoothing the rhythm of the line. Everything else in the verse is accurate and reads well.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew miqqedem can mean "in the east," "toward the east," or (temporally) "from of old, in the beginning." Rendering it "toward the east" keeps the spatial sense that fits the geography sketched in verses 10–14, while the phrasing leaves open whether the direction is measured from the narrator's vantage point or describes the garden's location within the wider region of Eden. Some older interpreters took the word temporally, "planted a garden in Eden from the first," and a few ancient versions reflect that reading. Note also the word order: Hebrew places the garden before the man, and the sentence is kept as two short clauses joined by "and" so that the reading voice can pause naturally at the comma. "Placed" translates a verb (wayyasem) that means simply "put, set"; a slightly stronger rendering such as "settled" or "stationed" would overreach.

The verb yittaʿ, "planted," is used elsewhere of a farmer or a king setting out vines and orchards, so God is pictured here as a gardener. Gan denotes an enclosed, cultivated, watered plot, not wild countryside. The name ʿEden sounds in Hebrew like the noun ʿeden, "delight, luxury" (compare the plural in expressions for pleasures), and later Hebrew and Greek tradition heard exactly that echo; many scholars connect the name instead with an Akkadian/Sumerian word for open plain or steppe. The chapter continues its wordplay from verse 7, where the man (ʾadam) is drawn from the ground (ʾadamah) and now set to dwell in a garden of that ground. The Masoretic text unusually joins gan to be-ʿEden with a linking hyphen, tying "garden" and "in Eden" tightly together.

Royal gardens with imported trees, canals and shade were a boast of ancient Near Eastern kings, symbols of prosperity, order and dominion; the picture of a deity planting such a park would have been immediately recognizable. Eden is placed vaguely "toward the east" from the perspective of the land of Israel, in the direction of the great river systems named in verses 10–14. The Greek translators rendered gan with a word borrowed from Persian for a walled royal park, which is the ancestor of the English word "paradise."

The garden is presented as a gift prepared before the man is put into it: provision precedes responsibility. Many readers see here temple imagery — a sacred space, planted by God, entered from the east, with life-giving water and guarded access (compare verse 9 and 3:24) — so that the garden becomes the first sanctuary where God and humanity are at home together. Interpretive traditions divide over whether Eden is presented as a real geographical location, a symbolic depiction of unspoiled communion with God, or both at once; the text itself is more interested in the relationship than in the map.

The ancient Greek version keeps both the place name and the eastward reference; the old Latin tradition read the name as the common noun and rendered "a garden of delight," and understood miqqedem temporally as "from the beginning." These are interpretive renderings of the same consonantal Hebrew text rather than evidence of a different underlying wording.

text: And out of the ground the LORD God made grow every tree pleasing to the sight and good for food, with the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

versions.text: Out of the ground the LORD God made every tree grow that is pleasing to the eye and good for food, and in the middle of the garden the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
versions.explanation: Two improvements for flow and fidelity: (1) 'made every tree grow that is pleasing to the eye' awkwardly splits the noun from its modifiers; 'made grow every tree pleasing to the sight and good for food' keeps the pair of descriptions together and reads better aloud. (2) The Hebrew places the tree of life first and its location second ('and the tree of life in the middle of the garden'); restoring that order keeps the two trees parallel at the end of the verse and avoids the fronted 'and in the middle of the garden.' The opening 'And' also matches the waw-consecutive rhythm of the surrounding verses.

footnotes.text: The verb is a causative (hiphil) form of the root meaning "to sprout": God does not merely plant but "causes to sprout," rendered here "made grow" to keep a natural English rhythm while preserving the sense that the growth is God's doing. "Pleasing to the sight" renders a passive participle meaning "desirable, delightful"; alternatives include "desirable to look at" or "a delight to the eyes." The Hebrew simply strings the last two items on with "and" ("and the tree of life... and the tree of the knowledge..."); this reading uses "with" for the first of them, marking that these two trees are singled out from among "every tree" already mentioned, and avoiding a chain of three identical connectives that would drag when read aloud. "The tree of the knowledge of good and evil" keeps the traditional wording; the Hebrew noun is verbal in force, so "the tree of knowing good and evil" is equally defensible.

"The ground" is 'adamah, the same word from which the man ('adam) was formed in v. 7; the trees and the human being share one origin, a play on words the Hebrew keeps sounding throughout these chapters. The participle "pleasing" comes from the root ḥ-m-d, "to covet, desire" — the same root that stands behind the prohibition on coveting and that reappears when the woman sees that the tree is "desirable" (3:6). The phrase "good and evil" is a merism: naming the two poles to include everything between them, much as "heaven and earth" means the whole cosmos. "In the middle" (be-tokh) can mean the exact center or simply "among, within"; the grammar leaves open whether one tree or both stand at the center (compare 3:3).

Two trees, two questions. The tree of life stands for a life that does not end, a gift withheld after the expulsion (3:22-24) and promised again at the close of Scripture. What the second tree offers is debated: moral discernment, the autonomy to decide good and evil for oneself, comprehensive knowledge, or the passage from innocence into adult experience. On any reading, the issue is not knowledge as such — God calls creation "good" and gives the man work and speech — but knowledge seized apart from trust. The trees are named here, before any command, so that the reader knows what is at stake long before the serpent speaks. Later wisdom writing calls wisdom itself "a tree of life" (Proverbs 3:18), and Christian tradition has long read the cross and the tree of life together.

Kings of the ancient Near East planted irrigated pleasure-parks stocked with exotic trees, both ornamental and fruit-bearing; royal inscriptions boast of them in the very terms used here — beautiful to look at and good to eat. Sacred trees flanked by guardian figures are a common motif in the art of Mesopotamia and Syria-Palestine. The search for a plant that confers unending life also drives the Mesopotamian Gilgamesh epic, where the hero finds the plant and then loses it to a serpent — a striking parallel in imagery, though the biblical account puts the question of life in wholly different terms.

The ancient versions support the received Hebrew text here. The early Greek translation expands slightly on the second tree, rendering it "the tree of knowing what is knowable of good and evil," an interpretive touch rather than evidence of a different Hebrew reading. The Samaritan text agrees substantially with the traditional Hebrew.

This passage belongs to the creation readings used at the great vigil of Easter in many traditions, and it is often paired in Lenten lectionaries with the account of the temptation, so that the naming of the two trees is heard just before the story of the choice made between them.

text: Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided and became four headwaters.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew uses a participle ("going out") with no definite article, describing an ongoing state rather than a single event; English narrative rhythm favors the simple past, "A river flowed out of Eden." Some render it in the present ("a river goes out") to keep the timeless feel of the description. The final phrase is literally "and became four heads"; since Hebrew rōʾš can mean the source or beginning of a stream, "headwaters" is used here rather than the more ambiguous "heads" or the interpretive "branches." The verb translated "divided" is reflexive in form — the river "parted itself" — and could also be rendered "separated into channels."

Nāhār is the ordinary word for a perennial river (as opposed to a seasonal wadi). The verb yippārēd is the passive-reflexive (niphal) stem of a root used elsewhere for people or groups separating from one another, so the river's splitting is described in language normally used for parting company. Rōʾš, "head," carries a rich range: chief, beginning, summit, and — as here — the source or main stream of a watercourse. The name Eden resonates with a Hebrew word for delight or luxury, though many connect it with an older Near Eastern term for steppe or plain; the text itself plays on the sense of pleasure.

In ancient Near Eastern imagination, a single spring or river issuing from a sacred mountain or garden and dividing to water the world was a familiar picture of fertility and divine provision. Two of the four rivers named in the following verses (the Tigris and the Euphrates) are well known; the identity of the other two has been debated since antiquity, with proposals ranging from canals in Mesopotamia to river systems in Arabia, Persia, or Africa. The description places Eden at the origin of the known waters rather than at a locatable point on a map.

The river rising in Eden and going out to the wider world presents the garden as the source of life for all lands, not a private enclosure. This imagery is picked up by later prophets and visionaries, who describe water flowing from the sanctuary or from God's throne to heal the nations — so that the end of the story returns to its beginning. The single river becoming four has also been read as a picture of blessing spreading to the whole earth, the number four suggesting the four directions or the totality of the world.

versions.text: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided and became four headwaters.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew clause opens with a disjunctive waw plus a fronted noun (we-nahar yotse'), marking a shift from the narrative sequence to a descriptive aside about the garden's geography. Rendering it 'Now a river...' signals that break for the listener and sets this verse apart from the waw-consecutive narration of the preceding verses, while keeping the oral rhythm smooth.

text: The name of the first is Pishon; it winds around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.

versions.text: The name of the first is Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew participle הַסֹּבֵב means to encircle or go around; "winds through" suggests passing across the interior rather than encompassing the territory. "Winds around" keeps the same natural rhythm while matching the sense of the verb.

footnotes.text: Hebrew literally has "the name of the one is Pishon"; since the previous verse speaks of four headwaters, "the first" is the natural English idiom for beginning an enumeration, and it keeps the line short for reading aloud. The verb here is a participle ("the one going around/encircling"), a form that describes an enduring state rather than a past event; hence the present tense "winds around" even though verse 10 was rendered in the past. "Winds around" was chosen over the flatter "encircles" or "goes around" because it suggests a river's meandering course while preserving the sense of surrounding or skirting the whole territory. The closing clause is a simple relative construction, "which there the gold," with no verb; "where there is gold" supplies the verb English requires. The proper names Pishon and Havilah are transliterated rather than translated, as their meanings are uncertain.

The name Pishon (pîšôn) has been connected to a root meaning to leap, spread out, or gush, which would suit a river in flood, though the etymology is not certain. Havilah (ḥăwîlâ) is often linked to ḥôl, "sand," suggesting a sandy or desert region. The participle hassōvēv comes from the root s-b-b, "to turn, go around, surround" — the same root behind words for a circuit or a circle; it can mean either to encircle completely or to skirt along the edge of something. The object marker ʾēt before "the whole land" is unusual after a participle and adds a certain weight to the phrase.

Havilah appears elsewhere in the genealogies as both a descendant of Cush and a descendant of Joktan, and as a region on the fringe of Arabia. Gold-bearing regions of Arabia and Nubia were famous in antiquity, and gold, aromatic resins, and precious stones (see the next verse) were classic luxury imports along the caravan routes. Ancient and modern readers have located the Pishon in places as far apart as India and Arabia; one proposal identifies it with a now-dry riverbed running from the Arabian highlands toward the Persian Gulf. No identification commands general agreement.

The naming of real, locatable rivers and lands roots the garden in the geography of the known world rather than in pure myth; at the same time the four branches flowing out to the corners of the earth present Eden as the source of the world's life and abundance. The listing of gold, and in the next verse bdellium and onyx, quietly anticipates the materials of the sanctuary and the priestly garments, so that the garden is portrayed as a kind of first temple whose wealth is later gathered up in Israel's worship.

The ancient Greek tradition renders the names as Pheison and Heuilat, and the early Latin as Phison and Hevilath; these are transliterations rather than variant readings. The consonantal Hebrew text is stable here, with no significant variants among the witnesses.

text: The gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx are also there.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew ends with two nouns joined by 'and': literally 'there is the bdellium and the onyx stone.' Since the verse continues the description of the land begun in verse 11 ('where there is gold'), the rendering places 'bdellium and onyx' first and adds 'also' to signal that these are further treasures of the same region; this keeps the sentence short and easy to speak aloud. Both substances are named with the definite article in Hebrew, which here marks them as well-known commodities rather than particular items, so English drops the article. 'Bdellium' keeps the traditional rendering of Hebrew bedolach, a word of uncertain meaning; it may denote an aromatic gum resin (the sense assumed here and reflected in the comparison of manna's appearance in Numbers 11:7) or possibly pearl or a whitish gemstone. 'Onyx' likewise renders shoham, another obscure term; carnelian, lapis lazuli, beryl, malachite and chrysoprase have all been proposed. Because the identifications cannot be settled, the long-established English names are retained. The Hebrew has no verb in either clause; 'is' and 'are' are supplied as the idiom requires.

The feminine demonstrative 'that' is spelled הַהִוא, with a waw where one would expect a yod — a distinctive orthography for the feminine pronoun found throughout the first five books, read as the feminine form even though it looks like the masculine. The word 'good' (tov) is the same term used repeatedly in the creation account, tying the quality of the land's gold to the goodness of what God has made. Note also the placement of shām ('there') at the head of the second clause for emphasis, echoing the same word at the end of verse 11.

Gold, aromatic resin and precious stone were the classic luxury goods of ancient long-distance trade, moving by caravan out of Arabia, Nubia and beyond. A listing like this identifies a region as fabulously rich, much as ancient inscriptions boast of tribute in gold and gemstones. The three commodities named here reappear together in the furnishing of Israel's sanctuary: gold overlays its structures, fragrant resins go into its incense, and shoham stones are set on the high priest's shoulder pieces and breastpiece (Exodus 25; 28; 30).

Readers have long noticed that the materials of the garden reappear in the tabernacle and temple, and again in the vision of the city of God with its gold and jewels. On this reading the garden is presented as the first sanctuary, and its wealth is not merely scenic detail but a sign of God's generous provision and of the beauty proper to a place where God and humanity meet. Others read the note more soberly, as geographical description meant to locate Eden in the real world rather than to symbolize anything.

The ancient Greek translation renders the two substances as 'carbuncle' (a red stone) and 'leek-green stone,' showing that the Hebrew terms were already unclear in antiquity. The early Latin version keeps 'bdellium' and 'onyx,' the tradition followed here. The consonantal Hebrew text itself is stable across the witnesses; only the identification of the materials is disputed.

text: The name of the second river is Gihon; it winds around the whole land of Cush.

versions.text: The name of the second river is Gihon; it winds through the whole land of Cush.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew participle הַסּוֹבֵב (from סבב) means to go around, encircle, or skirt, not to pass through. 'Winds around' preserves the encircling sense while keeping the smooth oral rhythm; the same rendering should be used in the parallel clause about the first river for consistency.

footnotes.text: The participle הַסּוֹבֵב (hassovev) describes an ongoing, characteristic action, so the present tense "winds around" fits both the Hebrew form and the flowing rhythm of the passage. The root means to encircle, surround, or go around; renderings such as "encircles," "flows around," or "meanders through" are equally defensible. "Winds around" was chosen over "encompasses" because it keeps the line short and speakable and suggests a river's curving course rather than a static boundary. The name כּוּשׁ (Kush) is left in its Hebrew form, Cush, rather than being modernized to "Ethiopia" or "Nubia," since the ancient territory does not correspond neatly to any present-day country. The verse deliberately mirrors verse 11 word for word in structure, and the translation preserves that parallel cadence.

גִּיחוֹן (Gichon) derives from the root גיח, "to burst forth, gush out" — the same verb used of water breaking forth and of a child emerging from the womb. The name therefore evokes a spring that surges up from the ground. The independent pronoun ה֣וּא ("it") before the participle is emphatic, marking a clause that identifies and distinguishes this river from the others; Hebrew narrative often uses this construction in geographical notes.

Cush in the Hebrew Bible most often designates the region south of Egypt, along the upper Nile — ancient Nubia. Some interpreters, noting that the other three rivers point toward Mesopotamia, connect this Cush instead with the Kassites or a district east of the Tigris, since the name appears in more than one geographical setting in the ancient world. Gihon is also the name of the spring outside Jerusalem where Solomon was anointed king, and later readers heard a resonance between the garden's river and the water that sustained the holy city.

The four rivers spread out from a single source in the garden, sketching a world watered from one center. Interpreters have read this both as a geographical claim about a real place and as a picture of Eden as the fountainhead of life for the whole earth. Later prophetic and apocalyptic visions of a river flowing from the temple or the throne draw on this image, so the naming of these streams became a seedbed for hope of a restored creation.

text: The name of the third river is Tigris; it runs east of Asshur. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew names are Ḥiddeqel and Perat; here they are given in their familiar forms, Tigris and Euphrates, since these are the rivers the ancient names denote. A more literal rendering would keep "Hiddekel" and "Perath." The phrase rendered "it runs east of Assyria" translates a participle plus the construct noun qidmat, literally "the one going (to) the front/east of Asshur"; because qedem can mean both "front" and "east," the clause may also be understood as "it flows in front of Asshur" or "toward the east of Asshur." "Runs" is chosen over "goes" or "flows" for natural rhythm in reading aloud, matching "winds around" in the previous verse. The last clause has no verb in Hebrew, only the pronoun hu functioning as a link: "and the fourth river, it (is) Perath"; the short English sentence preserves the abruptness of a name that needed no further description.

Ḥiddeqel reflects the Akkadian name Idiqlat (Sumerian Idigna), from which the Greek Tigris also derives; Perat corresponds to Akkadian Purattu, Greek Euphrates. Asshur (אַשּׁוּר) is used in the Hebrew Bible both for the city on the Tigris and for the wider land and empire of Assyria, so the geography is deliberately open. Note also the repeated participial construction ha-holek, "the one going," parallel to ha-sovev, "the one winding around," in verse 13, giving the four-river description a steady, patterned cadence.

Tigris and Euphrates were the great rivers of Mesopotamia, the heartland of the earliest cities and empires known to Israel. Asshur, the old capital on the west bank of the Tigris, lay in the region the river passes; the Euphrates was so central to the world of the ancient Near East that it is often called simply "the River" elsewhere in Scripture, which explains why it alone receives no geographical note here. For readers of the time, naming these two rivers anchored the garden's watercourses to real, known geography.

The two identifiable rivers ground the garden in the known world, while the first two (Pishon and Gihon) remain elusive. Interpreters have read this in different ways: some take the passage as describing an actual location later lost or reshaped, others as portraying Eden as the source of the world's life-giving waters, a mountain sanctuary from which blessing flows to all lands. The image of a river watering the world recurs in prophetic and visionary texts about God's dwelling place.

Ancient translations render the Assyria clause variously: the Greek tradition reads "it flows opposite the Assyrians," and some later versions "over against Assyria," reflecting the ambiguity of qidmat rather than a different Hebrew text. The consonantal Hebrew itself is stable in the manuscript tradition.

versions.text: The name of the third river is Tigris; it runs east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew אַשּׁוּר at this point in the narrative most plausibly denotes the city of Asshur on the Tigris (the Assyrian empire lies far in the future within the story world), and the footnote itself notes the geography is 'deliberately open.' Rendering it 'Asshur' preserves that openness; if 'Assyria' is retained, no change is needed, but the transliterated form is more faithful to the ambiguity described in the notes.

text: The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.

footnotes.text: The verb rendered "settled" (wayyanniḥēhū) is not the same word used in verse 8, where God "planted" the garden and "put" the man there; here a different root is used, one connected with rest and secure placement. "Settled him" was chosen over the flatter "put him" to catch that sense of being given a place to stay. The pair of purpose clauses, "to work it and keep it," keeps the tight two-beat rhythm of the Hebrew (lěʿābdāh ūlěšāmrāh); alternatives include "to till it and tend it," "to cultivate and guard it," or, drawing out the cultic overtones of the two verbs, "to serve and to watch over." The definite "the man" preserves the Hebrew article on hāʾādām, which still functions here more as a designation of the human creature than as a personal name.

The verb ʿābad covers both agricultural labor ("work, till") and service rendered to a master or to God ("serve, worship"); šāmar means "keep, guard, watch over, observe." Both verbs carry a double register that English cannot hold in a single word. A grammatical curiosity: the pronoun suffixes on both infinitives are feminine ("it" = her), while "garden" (gan) is masculine. Explanations include an implied feminine antecedent such as "ground" (ʾădāmāh), an attraction to "Eden" understood as a place-name, or an idiomatic feminine used loosely for land or locality. Note also the sound play between ʾādām (man) and ʾădāmāh (ground) that runs through these chapters: the one taken from the soil is set to serve the soil.

The same verb pair, "serve and keep," is used elsewhere of the priests' and Levites' duties at the sanctuary and of keeping God's commandments. Many readers therefore hear the garden as a temple-like space and the human vocation as a priestly one: worshipful labor and faithful guarding. Two emphases follow. First, work is not a consequence of the fall but part of humanity's original calling and dignity; the toil of chapter 3 is a distortion of a good task, not its origin. Second, human dominion is stewardship: the man is placed in a garden he did not plant and is charged to tend and protect it, which has become a foundational text for reflection on care of creation.

Royal parks and irrigated pleasure gardens were a mark of kingship across the ancient Near East; rulers boasted of planting orchards, channeling water, and stocking them with trees from distant lands. An audience familiar with such gardens would recognize the picture: a well-watered enclosure with a keeper set over it. But the arrangement here is striking — the human is not the owner enjoying the estate but the gardener entrusted with it, dwelling in a place belonging to another.

The ancient Greek version renders the pronouns as masculine, agreeing with its word for "garden/paradise," thereby smoothing over the feminine suffixes of the Hebrew; some ancient witnesses and versions similarly harmonize. The consonantal Hebrew text is stable, and the feminine forms are best retained as original rather than corrected.

This verse is a fixture in readings and prayers on work, vocation, and the care of the earth, including harvest and planting observances, and is frequently paired with the creation account of chapter 1 in services celebrating human labor as a share in God's own work.

text: The LORD God commanded the man, "You may freely eat from every tree of the garden,

versions.text: And the LORD God commanded the man, "You are free to eat from any tree of the garden,
versions.explanation: Two small refinements for consistency and fidelity: (1) the preceding verse renders the same narrative verb form without an initial "And," so dropping it here keeps the narrative voice uniform and reads more cleanly aloud; (2) "may freely eat" captures the emphatic infinitive-absolute construction (akhol tokhel) and pairs rhythmically with "you will surely die" in the next verse, where the same doubling occurs. "Every tree" also matches mikkol more closely while keeping the permissive sense natural in speech.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew has a redundant "saying" (le'mor) after the verb "commanded"; in English the quotation marks carry that function, so it is left untranslated. The Hebrew preposition after "commanded" is literally "upon/concerning the man" — a construction that stresses a charge laid upon someone under authority; "commanded the man" renders the sense idiomatically. The doubled verb form (an infinitive absolute with the finite verb) is emphatic and here strengthens a permission, hence "you may freely eat"; alternatives include "you may certainly eat" or "you may eat to your heart's content." The verse is left open with a comma because the command runs unbroken into the next verse: one speech, two halves.

The pairing 'akhol to'khel ("eating you shall eat") in this verse is deliberately echoed by mot tamut ("dying you shall die") in the next — the same emphatic doubling used first for liberty and then for consequence. Hebrew 'ets covers both "tree" and "wood"; "every tree of the garden" is a collective singular, best read as "all the trees."

The order of the words matters: an expansive gift comes before any restriction. The single prohibition of the next verse is framed by generosity, not by scarcity. Readers have long noted that this is the first divine command addressed to humanity, and that it presupposes a creature capable of hearing, trusting, and choosing — the ground of later reflection on human freedom and responsibility.

The scene resembles ancient Near Eastern grants in which a king assigns land or a garden estate to a servant, with the gift secured by a single stipulation that acknowledges the giver's sovereignty. Royal parks and irrigated pleasure gardens, stocked with fruit trees and entrusted to a keeper, were a familiar image of ordered abundance in Mesopotamia and Egypt.

The traditional Hebrew text is stable here. Ancient Greek witnesses render the emphatic Hebrew doubling with a cognate noun plus verb ("with eating you shall eat"), confirming that the construction was understood as intensive; some Greek copies add "for food," a clarifying expansion rather than a different reading.

text: but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for on the day you eat from it you will surely die."

footnotes.text: The phrase rendered "you will surely die" translates a Hebrew construction that doubles the verb (literally "dying you shall die"), an emphatic idiom. Options include "you shall certainly die," "you will die for sure," or the older, wooden "dying thou shalt die." The reading chosen keeps the force of the emphasis while sounding natural when spoken aloud. "On the day you eat" preserves the literal Hebrew wording; the same phrase frequently functions simply as "when" or "as soon as," so a rendering like "when you eat from it" would also be defensible, but the concrete "day" language is retained because it becomes important to how the story unfolds. The verse continues the quotation begun in the previous verse, and "but" marks the contrast with the sweeping permission just granted.

The Hebrew joins two clauses with a simple "and" ("and from the tree..."), which in context is adversative — hence "but." The negative used with the imperfect verb expresses an absolute, standing prohibition rather than a one-time command. "The knowledge of good and evil" uses a pair of opposites to express totality, a figure of speech in which two extremes stand for everything in between; the noun "knowledge" comes from a root that covers not merely information but experience, intimacy, and the capacity to discern. Note also the sound-play running through the passage: the words for "tree," "eat," and the repeated "from it" knit the command tightly to the permission of the preceding verse.

Interpreters have long debated how the warning is fulfilled, since the man does not physically die on the day he eats. Proposals include: the death is spiritual or relational, an immediate estrangement from God; the phrase means "you will become subject to death," mortality entering as a certainty; the sentence is passed on that very day though its execution is delayed by mercy; or "in the day" is simply idiomatic for "when" and carries no strict same-day timetable. The prohibition also raises the question of what the knowledge of good and evil represents — moral discernment, adult wisdom, or the self-appointed authority to decide for oneself what is good and what is evil. What is clear is that the command establishes human life as answerable to God: freedom is vast ("every tree"), yet real, with a boundary that makes obedience meaningful.

Ancient Near Eastern law and treaty texts commonly paired a grant of benefits with a stipulation and a stated penalty, and the pattern of generous provision, single restriction, and death sentence would have sounded familiar to early hearers. Tree imagery — trees of life, plants of rejuvenation, and forbidden knowledge — appears in other ancient stories of the region, though here the trees stand within a relationship between a personal God and the human he has placed in the garden.

The traditional Hebrew text is stable here. Early Greek and Latin versions render the doubled Hebrew verb literally ("by death you shall die"), reflecting the same underlying wording rather than a different text. Some ancient witnesses harmonize small details of the command with its later restatements in the narrative, where the woman recounts it with the added words "nor shall you touch it"; those additions are secondary and are not reflected here.

text: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper suitable for him."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew phrase 'ezer kenegdo is notoriously difficult to render in a single English expression. 'Ezer means 'help' or 'helper' — one who supplies what is lacking — while kenegdo is built from the preposition 'like/as' plus 'in front of, opposite,' yielding something like 'corresponding to him' or 'his counterpart.' 'A helper suitable for him' aims for a natural, readable phrase that keeps both ideas: real assistance, and a match of equal standing. Other defensible renderings include 'a helper corresponding to him,' 'a partner fit for him,' or 'a helper as his counterpart.' The older wording 'help meet for him' (that is, 'help fitting for him') lies behind the English noun 'helpmeet,' which is a misreading of two separate words. 'The man' translates ha-adam with the definite article, so it is not yet a personal name here. 'I will make' renders a first-person singular verb; the reading behind some ancient versions is plural ('let us make'), noted below.

'Ezer derives from a root meaning to help, aid, or rescue, and in Hebrew it carries no implication of inferiority or subordinate rank. Kenegdo joins ke- ('like, as') with neged ('in front of, opposite, over against'), plus the pronominal suffix: literally 'like what is opposite him.' The image is of one standing face to face, matching and answering to the other — neither identical nor subordinate, but corresponding. Note also the deliberate echo of the chapter's refrain: after the repeated 'good' of the creation account, the divine assessment here is lo-tov, 'not good,' the first negative verdict in the Bible. The word tov ('good') also links back to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the preceding verse. The verb form 'e'esseh in the Masoretic Text carries an unusual mappiq in the final he, a scribal peculiarity noted by the medieval Masoretes.

The Masoretic Text reads a first-person singular verb, 'I will make.' The Samaritan Pentateuch and the ancient Greek translation instead read a plural, 'let us make,' harmonizing with the divine plural of the first creation account. The singular is the harder and better-attested reading and is followed here. Some Greek witnesses also render the closing phrase 'a helper like him' or 'according to him,' reflecting the difficulty of kenegdo already in antiquity; the Latin tradition's 'a help similar to him' shows the same struggle.

This is the first thing in Scripture declared 'not good,' and it concerns human solitude rather than any moral fault. Readers have drawn from it a theology of human beings as inherently relational, made for community. The word 'ezer is used elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible chiefly of God himself as Israel's help and deliverer, which has led many interpreters to insist that 'helper' here implies strength and rescue, not servitude. Interpretive traditions differ over whether kenegdo emphasizes equality and mutuality, complementary difference, or an ordered partnership; the Hebrew itself holds correspondence and distinction together without settling the question. The verse is also foundational for Jewish and Christian teaching on marriage and companionship.

In the ancient Near East, human beings in creation stories are typically fashioned to relieve the gods of labor; here, by contrast, the deity acts to relieve the human being's isolation. Household and kinship structures in the ancient world made solitary existence precarious — survival, land, and lineage all depended on a joined household — so the divine concern expressed here would have sounded practical as well as tender to its first hearers. The following verses stage a search among the animals that comes up empty, heightening the significance of the counterpart finally provided.

text: Now the LORD God had formed out of the ground every beast of the field and every bird of the sky, and he brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.

versions.text: Now the LORD God had formed out of the ground every beast of the field and every bird of the sky, and he brought them to the man to see what he would call them; and whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.
versions.explanation: The verse currently runs as a single long sentence joined by a semicolon, which is hard to sustain in one breath when read aloud. Breaking it into two sentences at the semicolon preserves the Hebrew's two movements (God forms and brings; the man names) and gives the closing clause the weight of a summary statement. Wording is otherwise accurate: the pluperfect 'had formed' appropriately handles the narrative sequence, and 'every beast of the field'/'every bird of the sky' renders the Hebrew closely.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb form here (wayyiqtol, "and he formed") normally carries the narrative forward, which would place the making of the animals after the man was created. Because the sequence in chapter 1 has the animals made before humanity, many render the verb as a pluperfect, "had formed," understood as a summary looking back rather than a new step in time; Hebrew narrative allows this when a clause supplies background. The word "Now" at the start signals that this is background information. Others keep a simple past, "formed," and read chapter 2 as an independent account with its own order. Hebrew leaves the object of "brought" unexpressed, so "them" is supplied for English. The final clause is literally "and everything that the man called it — a living creature — that was its name"; the rendering "whatever the man called each living creature" smooths a compressed construction that can also be read "whatever the man called it, that living creature, that was its name."

The verb yatsar means to shape or mold, and is used of a potter working clay; the same verb described the forming of the man in verse 7, underlining that animals and human being are made of the same stuff. "Out of the ground" is min-ha'adamah, echoing ha'adam, "the man" — a sound-play running through the chapter (earth-creature from the earth). Nephesh chayyah, "living creature" or "living being," is the very phrase applied to the man in verse 7, so the animals share his creaturely life even while none of them proves to be his match. The idiom qara le- ("call to/for") means to give a name to.

In the ancient Near East the right to name was an exercise of authority and discernment: kings named conquered cities, and gods named what they brought into being. The man's naming of the animals is therefore commonly read as his stewardship over creation being put into practice, and also as an act of insight — he perceives the nature of each creature. Note that God does not name the animals himself but defers to the man's judgment: "whatever the man called it, that was its name." Some interpreters also see the naming as a search: as the man surveys every living creature, the absence of a counterpart becomes plain, preparing for verses 20-23.

Naming lists were a real intellectual genre in the ancient world; Mesopotamian and Egyptian scribes compiled long catalogues of animals, plants, and stones. A reader in that world would recognize the man's naming as the work of a wise ruler and scholar, not merely a labeling exercise. Wild animals and birds are named here as the categories nearest to hand for such a survey.

The traditional Hebrew text lists "every beast of the field and every bird of the sky." Some ancient witnesses, including the Greek and Samaritan traditions, also mention the domestic animals here, harmonizing with the fuller list in verse 20; the shorter reading is generally preferred as original. The Greek translation renders the opening verb with a word suggesting "formed also/still," which shows that ancient readers already wrestled with how this verse relates in time to chapter 1.

text: So the man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every beast of the field. But for himself the man found no suitable helper.

versions.text: So the man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every beast of the field. But for the man no suitable helper was found.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb מָצָא is active third-person masculine singular ("he found"), continuing the man as subject; the passive "was found" obscures this. Adding "himself" also conveys the contrastive force of וּלְאָדָם at the head of the clause (naming was possible for every creature, but no counterpart emerged for the man), and the shorter ending reads more crisply aloud.

versions.text: So the man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every beast of the field. But for the man himself he found no suitable helper.
versions.explanation: The clause "for the man himself he found" is momentarily confusing when heard aloud, since "he" and "the man" are the same person, and a listener may briefly take "he" to be God. Placing "for himself" first keeps the Hebrew's fronted contrast (וּלְאָדָם) and retains the active verb with the man as subject, while removing the ambiguity of the double reference.

footnotes.text: The verse divides into two unequal halves, and the translation preserves that shape for the ear: three quick phrases of naming, then a sudden turn. Hebrew *behemah* here is rendered "livestock" (domestic animals) rather than "beasts," since the second half of the list already names "every beast of the field" (*chayyat hassadeh*), the same phrase used in the previous verse; "cattle" and "animals" are also possible. The closing clause reads literally "and for the man he did not find a helper corresponding to him": the Hebrew fronts "for the man" for contrast, and the added "himself" carries that emphasis into English rhythm. Because *le'adam* here lacks the definite article, it could also be read as the personal name, "but for Adam"; the translation keeps "the man" for consistency with the surrounding verses, where the article is present. "Suitable helper" renders *'ezer kenegdo*; alternatives include "a helper corresponding to him," "a helper as his counterpart," or "a partner fit for him."

*'Ezer* means "help" or "helper" and elsewhere in Scripture most often describes God as the help of his people, so the word by itself implies nothing lowly. *Kenegdo* is built on *neged*, "in front of, opposite, over against," with the preposition *ke-*, "like, according to": one who stands face to face with him, matching him. The pair therefore suggests correspondence and equality rather than mere assistance. Note also the ongoing sound-play in the chapter between *'adam* (man) and *'adamah* (ground) from which the animals were formed — the creatures share his origin but not his likeness. The verb "he found" (*matsa'*) implies an actual search among the named creatures, not simply an absence.

Naming in the Hebrew Bible expresses discernment and stewardship: to name is to know a thing's nature and to exercise authority given by God. The man's naming of the animals thus continues the mandate of dominion, but it also functions as a kind of examination that ends in lack — a divinely arranged discovery that the man is alone in a way no animal can remedy. Interpreters have long debated the force of "helper corresponding to him": some read it as indicating a partner equal in nature and complementary in role, others have drawn from it arguments about ordering within marriage, often in conversation with later apostolic reflection on the creation accounts. The verse also stands as the first note of insufficiency in a chapter otherwise full of blessing, preparing for the only creative act God performs after declaring something "not good."

Lists of animals grouped by class (domestic herds, birds, wild game) were a familiar scholarly genre in the ancient Near East, where scribes compiled catalogues of creatures, plants and stones. Ancient readers would have recognized the man's naming as an act of wisdom of the kind attributed to kings and sages, who were praised for mastering such lists. The threefold grouping here — livestock, birds of the sky, beasts of the field — reflects the everyday categories of an agrarian society rather than a systematic zoology.

Some ancient witnesses render the final clause in the passive, "but for Adam there was found no helper like him," smoothing the abrupt shift of subject in the Hebrew, and some read the personal name Adam here. The differences are matters of interpretation and idiom rather than a variant Hebrew text; the traditional Hebrew reading, with its unexpressed "he found," is followed here.

text: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept, he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.

versions.text: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.
versions.explanation: The rendering is accurate and reads well. For oral delivery, a comma after the introductory clause 'and while he slept' gives the reader a natural breath point and prevents the run-on feel of 'and while he slept he took.' (An alternative closer to the Hebrew's chain of verbs would be 'and he slept; and he took one of his ribs...', but the present phrasing flows better aloud.)

footnotes.text: The verse opens with a chain of Hebrew verbs joined by "and" (literally: "and the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and he slept, and he took..."). For oral reading the second clause has been folded into a temporal phrase, "and while he slept," which preserves the sequence without the monotony of repeated "and." The Hebrew ṣelaʿ is rendered "rib" here, following the oldest interpretive tradition; "side" is an equally defensible rendering, and "one of his sides" is favoured by some interpreters (see the note on the vocabulary). The final phrase taḥtennāh means literally "underneath it" or "in its place"; "in its place" is chosen because English "underneath" would suggest a layer of flesh below the rib rather than the closing of the gap left by its removal. Note also that "the man" translates hā-ʾādām with the article — a designation of the human being, not yet a personal name.

Tardēmāh, "deep sleep," comes from the root r-d-m and denotes a heavy, God-given torpor rather than ordinary sleep; the same word falls on Abram at the covenant between the pieces and on Saul's camp when David slips past. It is regularly associated with divine action and revelation. Ṣelaʿ occurs some forty times in the Hebrew Bible and elsewhere almost always means "side" in an architectural sense — the sides of the ark, the boards or side-chambers of the tabernacle and temple, the flanks of a hill. This is the only place where it is taken of a part of the human body, which is why some read "one of his sides" rather than "one of his ribs." The verb sāgar, "to shut, close up," is the ordinary word for closing a door and is used here of closing the flesh over the wound.

The Greek tradition renders tardēmāh with a word meaning "trance" or "ecstasy," giving the sleep a visionary colouring, and translates the last clause as "and filled up flesh in its place" rather than "closed up." Whether this reflects a slightly different Hebrew reading or simply an interpretive rendering cannot be determined. The consonantal Hebrew text is otherwise stable across the manuscript tradition, including the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Judaean Desert scrolls.

That the man is asleep means he contributes nothing to the making of the woman: she is God's work, not his. Early Jewish commentary drew a lesson from the place of the rib — taken not from the head that she should rule over him, nor from the foot that she should be trampled, but from his side, that she should stand beside him. Christian interpreters from the second century onward read the sleep of the first man and the opening of his side as a figure of the death of Christ, from whose pierced side the church was said to be born. The passage has also carried heavy weight in debates about the relation of man and woman, though the immediate point of the narrative is sameness of substance rather than hierarchy, as the next verses make explicit.

Ancient Mesopotamian literature offers a suggestive parallel: in the Sumerian tale of Enki and Ninhursag, the god's ailing rib is healed by the goddess Ninti, whose name plays on the words for "rib" and "to live" — the same pairing that surfaces in Genesis when the woman is named Ḥawwāh, "living." Divinely induced sleep as the setting for a decisive act of the gods is a familiar motif in the literature of the ancient Near East. The description of the wound being closed over reflects the ordinary language of healing rather than any surgical technique.

The verse belongs to the opening Torah reading of the annual synagogue cycle. In Christian usage it is among the passages appointed for marriage services, where verses 18–24 are read together as the foundational text on the union of husband and wife.

text: Then the LORD God built the rib that he had taken from the man into a woman, and he brought her to the man.

versions.text: Then the LORD God built the rib he had taken from the man into a woman, and he brought her to the man.
versions.explanation: The rendering is accurate ('built... into a woman' preserves the Hebrew verb "banah" with the lamed of product). For oral reading, however, the long gap between 'built the rib' and its complement 'into a woman' can obscure the sense; adding the relative pronoun 'that' clearly marks the intervening clause and gives the sentence a smoother, more predictable cadence when read aloud.

footnotes.text: The verb rendered "built" is Hebrew wayyiben, from bānâ, the ordinary word for constructing a house, wall, or city. The literalness is preserved here because the image is deliberate: God is pictured as a craftsman-builder shaping the woman out of material taken from the man. Smoother renderings such as "formed," "made," or "fashioned" convey the sense but lose the architectural metaphor. The phrase le'ishshah is literally "to/for a woman" — the Hebrew preposition marks the result of the building, hence "into a woman"; it can also carry the nuance "as a wife," and some renderings bring that out. "The rib" follows verse 21, though the Hebrew noun can equally mean "side" (see the lingvistisk note). The final clause is unadorned in Hebrew — "and he brought her to the man" — and is kept short for the rhythm of the sentence and to set up the man's exclamation in the next verse.

Hebrew ṣēlāʿ is used elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible chiefly of the "sides" of architectural structures — the sides of the ark, the tabernacle, the temple, and its side chambers — and only here and in verse 21 of part of a human body. This architectural vocabulary pairs naturally with the verb bānâ, "build," in this verse. Note also that God "formed" (yāṣar, the potter's word) the man from dust in 2:7, but "builds" the woman from living human material — a variation in verbs that many read as significant rather than accidental. The wordplay of ʾishshâ ("woman") with ʾîsh ("man") is announced in the next verse, and the appearance of ʾishshâ here prepares for it.

The woman is not made from dust, as the man was, but from the man himself, and she is presented to him by God. Interpreters have drawn opposite conclusions from this: some see a derivation implying order or headship, others emphasize that she is of identical substance and therefore fully his equal, with the man's own words in the following verse serving as the recognition of that equality. The rabbinic reading of ṣēlāʿ as "side" supported a tradition that the first human was originally undifferentiated and was divided into two, so that marriage restores an original unity — an idea echoed in the "one flesh" of verse 24.
