That God himself brings her to the man has also long been read as the pattern for marriage as a divine gift rather than a human arrangement.

In the ancient Near East the father or guardian formally presented a bride to her husband; here God performs that role, and the language of "bringing her to the man" would have evoked the betrothal customs of the hearers. Other ancient creation accounts also speak of deities fashioning humans from clay or divine substance, but the deliberate making of a partner for an existing solitary human, and the intimate presentation that follows, has no close parallel.

The consonantal Hebrew text is stable here. The ancient Greek translation uses "built" (ōkodomēsen), confirming the architectural verb, and renders the object with a word meaning "side" or "rib." In the closing phrase the Hebrew has "the man" with the article; several ancient versions read the name Adam instead, a difference that in unpointed Hebrew involves no change of consonants.

With verses 18–24 this verse belongs to the classic marriage lection, read at wedding services in many Christian traditions and cited in Jewish wedding liturgy through the blessings that recall the joy of the first couple in Eden.

text: And the man said, "This one at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, for she was taken out of man."

versions.text: And the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, for she was taken out of man."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew "zot happa'am" points to the woman herself ("this one"), not to an abstract state; "This one at last" makes the referent explicit and reads more naturally aloud, since "This at last is bone of my bones" can momentarily sound like a comment on a situation rather than an exclamation about her. The rest of the verse, including the woman/man wordplay, is well rendered and rhythmically balanced.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally says "this, the time" (zoth happa'am), an idiom of emphatic recognition. It can be rendered "this time" (as opposed to the parade of animals in vv. 19-20, none of which matched), or "at last!" as a cry of relief and delight. The translation keeps both nuances with "This one at last," and the word order preserves the poetic rhythm of the Hebrew, which begins with the emphatic pronoun. The English "she shall be called woman" renders a passive verb form ("one shall call her," i.e. "her name shall be"); it announces a name rather than issuing a command. The closing line, "for she was taken out of man," uses a rare passive perfect; some prefer the smoother "because she was taken from the man," but the definite article is absent in Hebrew, so the more generic "man" is used, matching the generic "woman."

The Hebrew turns on the sound-play between 'ishshah (woman) and 'ish (man) — a pairing English can only approximate, since "woman" and "man" happen to echo each other in sound but not by the same route. Historically the two Hebrew words are probably not derived from one another (they appear to come from different roots), so this is a poetic "folk etymology": the likeness in sound is used to declare a likeness in nature. Note also that up to this point the text has used ha'adam, "the human being"; only here does 'ish, "man" as counterpart to woman, first appear.

"Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" is a fixed kinship formula elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, used when relatives or tribes acknowledge one another as belonging to the same family (compare Gen 29:14; Judg 9:2; 2 Sam 5:1; 19:12-13). It is therefore not merely a comment on anatomy but a declaration of covenant belonging: "you are my own flesh and blood."

These are the first recorded words of a human being in Scripture, and they are poetry. Interpreters have long noted that the man recognizes in the woman not a subordinate but a corresponding equal — the same stuff, the same nature — which many read as a foundation for the equal dignity of the sexes. The naming has also been read by others as an exercise of authority, parallel to the naming of the animals, though here the noun given is a category term rather than a personal name. The verse, with the one that follows, is taken up in New Testament teaching on marriage as the pattern for the union of husband and wife.

Ancient translations smooth the closing clause: the Greek reads "out of her man/husband," adding a possessive pronoun, and some witnesses similarly specify "the man." These are clarifying expansions; the shorter Hebrew wording, which leaves "man" indefinite and thus preserves the wordplay, is followed here.
With the following verse this passage is among the most frequently read texts in marriage liturgies, often paired with readings on love and covenant faithfulness.

text: That is why a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.

versions.text: That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife, and they become one flesh.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb (davaq) is active and conveys clinging or holding fast; the passive "is joined to" softens the image and shifts agency away from the man. "Holds fast to" preserves the active force, matches the parallel active verb "leaves," and reads with a stronger oral cadence.

footnotes.text: "That is why" renders the Hebrew ʿal-ken, a standard formula by which the narrator steps out of the story to explain a present-day custom; the whole verse is a narrator's aside, not words spoken by the man. The Hebrew verbs are non-past forms describing what typically happens, so they are rendered as English simple present ("leaves… holds fast… become"), giving a timeless, proverbial sense; other renderings take them as future or obligatory ("shall leave… shall cleave"). "Holds fast to" translates davaq, elsewhere often "cleave" or "cling"; the older word "cleave" is avoided because in modern English it also means to split apart. Hebrew repeats the object marker before each parent ("his father and his mother"), but English reads more naturally with a single possessive, and the compact phrasing suits reading aloud. "One flesh" preserves the Hebrew image literally rather than paraphrasing it as "one body" or "one family."

The verse continues the sound-play of the preceding verse: ish ("man") and ishshah ("woman/wife") stand at either end of the sentence, so that the man who leaves as ish is joined to his ishshah. The verb davaq means literally to stick or be glued to something; it describes a tongue sticking to the palate, skin clinging to bone, or soldiers pressing after an enemy. It is also the classic covenant word for loyal attachment — Israel is commanded to "hold fast" to the LORD. "Flesh" (basar) in Hebrew can denote not only the physical body but kinship and blood relationship, as in the phrase "our own flesh." "One" (echad) is the same word used for unity elsewhere, and here forms a striking pair with the plural verb: "they become one."

In the ancient Near East marriage was normally patrilocal: the bride left her household and joined her husband's family, and the husband's father retained authority over the household. The verse deliberately reverses that expectation, saying that the man is the one who leaves — a rhetorical way of stressing that the marriage bond outweighs even the strongest claims of parentage and lineage. "Leaving" here is not a legal statement about residence but about the transfer of primary loyalty. The language of clinging and of shared flesh also belongs to the vocabulary of kinship covenants, by which two parties who were not blood relatives declared themselves to be bone and flesh of one another.

This verse has carried enormous doctrinal weight as the foundational statement about marriage: it is presented as rooted in creation itself rather than in later law or custom. In the Gospels it is cited, together with the previous chapter's "male and female," as the reason marriage should not be dissolved; the argument turns on the permanence implied by "one flesh." Elsewhere it is quoted to argue that sexual union creates a real bond and not a casual act, and again to describe the union of Christ and the church as a "great mystery." Interpreters debate how far "one flesh" refers to sexual union, to the shared life of a household, or to the offspring in whom the two literally become one flesh; most read it as embracing all of these. Many also see in the singular "a man… his wife" an implicit norm of monogamy.

The traditional Hebrew text reads simply "and they become one flesh." The Samaritan version, the ancient Greek, Syriac and Latin translations all read "and the two become one flesh," and it is in this fuller form that the verse is quoted in the New Testament. The added "the two" may reflect a slightly different Hebrew text, or it may be an early clarifying expansion; it makes explicit what the Hebrew already implies. The translation follows the traditional Hebrew wording.

The verse is among the most frequently read texts in wedding services across Christian traditions, commonly paired with the preceding verse and often echoed in the words of joining and in the declaration that what God has united no one should separate.

text: The man and his wife were both naked, and they felt no shame.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word order is literally "And the two of them were naked, the man and his wife" — the subject is named after the verb and the pronoun, a common Hebrew pattern. For a smoother spoken line the translation places "The man and his wife" first and folds "the two of them" into the word "both." "The man" renders ha-adam with its definite article: at this point it is still a common noun, the human being, not yet used as the personal name Adam. The final clause could be rendered "and they were not ashamed" or "and they felt no shame before each other"; "they felt no shame" keeps the sentence short and rhythmic while preserving the sense of an ongoing, untroubled state rather than a single moment.

The word for "naked" here, arummim, is nearly identical in sound to arum, "shrewd, crafty," the word used of the serpent in the very next sentence of the story. The narrator is setting up a pun: the naked pair meet the shrewd creature. After the fruit is eaten a slightly different spelling, erummim, is used for their nakedness, marking the change in how they experience it. The verb translated "felt no shame" is a rare intensive-reflexive form of the root b-w-sh, which can carry a reciprocal sense — they were not ashamed in each other's presence.

The verse is the hinge between creation and the fall. Nakedness without shame pictures a state of complete openness — before God and before one another — with nothing hidden and nothing to hide. Interpreters have read this as innocence, as integrity, or as the absence of the self-consciousness that guilt produces; in each reading the loss described in chapter 3, where the same pair sew coverings and hide, measures exactly what has been broken. Read together with the preceding verse, the line also frames marital union as unashamed, God-given, and good.

In the ancient Near East public nakedness was normally associated with poverty, captivity, humiliation, or shame; captives and the destitute are regularly portrayed unclothed in texts and reliefs. Against that background the note that the first couple were naked "and felt no shame" would strike ancient hearers as remarkable — a description of a world before the social order in which clothing signalled status, dignity, and protection.

The ancient versions agree closely with the received Hebrew text here; the early Greek translation renders it straightforwardly as "and the two were naked... and they were not ashamed." The chapter break after this verse is a later editorial division: in the flow of the narrative the sentence belongs tightly with what follows, since the pun on "naked" and "crafty" runs straight across it.
